after.problem: If $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{7}$ and ${0}^{∘}<\theta <{90}^{∘}$ then what is the value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ?$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941628/assets/9d9aa1e6ffac387c53c7a1b35217a51cd17db7242ddedec4ff72c229a73d5291.png)

We're given that $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{7}.$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{3}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{40}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}.$

content.problem: If $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{7}$ and ${0}^{∘}<\theta <{90}^{∘}$ then what is the value of $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ?$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941628/assets/9d9aa1e6ffac387c53c7a1b35217a51cd17db7242ddedec4ff72c229a73d5291.png)

We're given that $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{7}.$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{7}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{3}{7})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{49}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{40}{49}} \\  & =\pm \frac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So, $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{7}.$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: If $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{5}{3}$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}<\theta <\pi $ then what is the value of $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ?$
after.worked_solution:
As $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{5}{3}$ then $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }=\frac{3}{5}.$

Let's sketch our angle $\theta $ in the coordinate plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941628/assets/aaba5af0542d29ef91d4b0e17907a81e32bccc402c48b32c205e7298630b5bc0.png)

We're given that $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{5}$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{4}{5}.$

Finally, knowing that $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }$ we have:

- $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{(-\frac{4}{5})}{(\frac{3}{5})}=-\frac{4}{3}$

- $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{3}{5})}{(-\frac{4}{5})}=-\frac{3}{4}.$

Finally, we have

$\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =-\frac{4}{3}-\frac{3}{4}=-\frac{25}{12}.$

EXPLANATION

As csc⁡θ=53 then sin⁡θ=1csc⁡θ=35.

Let's sketch our angle θ in the coordinate plane.

We're given that sin⁡θ=35 We can use the Pythagorean identity to find cos⁡θ:

sin2⁡θ+cos2⁡θ=1cos2⁡θ=1−sin2⁡θcos⁡θ=±1−sin2⁡θ

Substituting sin⁡θ=35 gives

cos⁡θ=±1−(35)2=±1−925=±1625=±45.

We select the negative answer since cos⁡θ is negative in the second quadrant. So, cos⁡θ=−45.

Finally, knowing that cot⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ, and tan⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ we have:

  • cot⁡θ=(−45)(35)=−43

  • tan⁡θ=(35)(−45)=−34.

Finally, we have

tan⁡θ+cot⁡θ=−43−34=−2512.

content.problem: If $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{5}{3}$ and $\frac{\pi }{2}<\theta <\pi $ then what is the value of $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta ?$
content.worked_solution:
As $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{5}{3}$ then $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta }=\frac{3}{5}.$

Let's sketch our angle $\theta $ in the coordinate plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941628/assets/aaba5af0542d29ef91d4b0e17907a81e32bccc402c48b32c205e7298630b5bc0.png)

We're given that $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{5}$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{3}{5})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{16}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{4}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{4}{5}.$

Finally, knowing that $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ and $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }$ we have:

- $\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =\frac{(-\frac{4}{5})}{(\frac{3}{5})}=-\frac{4}{3}$

- $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{3}{5})}{(-\frac{4}{5})}=-\frac{3}{4}.$

Finally, we have

$\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta =-\frac{4}{3}-\frac{3}{4}=-\frac{25}{12}.$

after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941628/assets/38a739ca964d1e9cf343914ed0a66f58363ceb7acfe7c194daf2765c0b4bf4d5.png)

We're given that $x=-\frac{7}{9}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{7}{9}.$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{7}{9}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(-\frac{7}{9})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{49}{81}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{32}{81}} \\  & =\pm \frac{4\sqrt{2}}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the negative answer since $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ is negative in the third quadrant. So $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =-\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{9}.$

Finally, knowing that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(-\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{9})}=-\frac{9}{4\sqrt{2}}=-\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{8}.
$$

Question 4

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that sin⁡θ=14, what is the value of tan⁡θ?

a
tan⁡θ=−355
b
tan⁡θ=−322
c
tan⁡θ=−1515
d
tan⁡θ=1515
e
tan⁡θ=355
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find cos⁡θ:

sin2⁡θ+cos2⁡θ=1cos2⁡θ=1−sin2⁡θcos⁡θ=±1−sin2⁡θ

Substituting sin⁡θ=14 gives

cos⁡θ=±1−(14)2=±1−116=±1516=±154.

We select the negative answer since cos⁡θ is negative in the second quadrant. So, cos⁡θ=−154.

Finally, knowing that tan⁡θ=sin⁡θcos⁡θ, we have tan⁡θ=(14)(−154)=−115=−1515.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms that θ is in quadrant II, so cosθ = −√(1 − 1/16) = −√15/4. Hence tanθ = (1/4)/(−√15/4) = −√15/15, matching option c.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941628/assets/cd41c969aee2e7c04c9034106978d8522d6a715733098bfde87abbdb861da7a8.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{4},$ what is the value of $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ?$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941628/assets/4942cec8983dd2bddddd0ba2f8f9332b1b82f3999a44adb138b905457d39c633.png)

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{16}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{15}{16}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ is negative in the second quadrant. So, $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4}.$

Finally, knowing that $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta =\frac{(\frac{1}{4})}{(-\frac{\sqrt{15}}{4})}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}}=-\frac{\sqrt{15}}{15}.
$$

after.problem: If $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{9}{10}$ and ${90}^{∘}<\theta <{180}^{∘}$ then what is the value of $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta ?$
after.worked_solution:
Let's sketch our angle $\theta $ in the coordinate plane.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13941628/assets/82ad5587912af9d07bf447281bba3eb714bfdfdf38fef529529956912b0a77ec.png)

We're given that $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{9}{10}.$ We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =-\frac{9}{10}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(-\frac{9}{10})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{81}{100}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{19}{100}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{19}}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the positive answer since $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ is positive in the second quadrant. So, $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{19}}{10}.$

Finally, knowing that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{(\frac{\sqrt{19}}{10})}=\frac{10}{\sqrt{19}}=\frac{10\sqrt{19}}{19}.
$$
